A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SpreadsheetArena study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated between sections.

before.justification: v1 reports 4,357 original preference votes, model rankings, feature regressions, failure analyses and a finance expert study covering 104 spreadsheets and 134 evaluations.

after.justification: v2 retains the original arena analyses and reports a revised finance study with 250 evaluations, a direct pairwise expert follow-up, and additional correlation and resource-use results.

M1.justification: The single-pass SheetSpec generation approach, matching algorithm, feature-augmented Bradley-Terry model, 29 features and failure-tagging pipeline are retained. The generation schema and judge prompt are unchanged; relocated explanations and revised evaluation studies do not establish a method change.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate spreadsheet generation across the same six workflow categories and retain the 436 seed prompts and 4,357-vote snapshot. v2 newly documents 1,033 prompts and their source/category distribution. The smaller finance-study sample changes sampling within existing coverage.

E2.justification: The same 16 models participate in the arena comparisons, and comparator membership in the academic and finance ranking tables is unchanged. Newly cited finance and spreadsheet systems are discussed as related work, not evaluated as additional baselines.

E3.justification: The finance study changes from 52 battles and 104 spreadsheets, mostly rated once, to 25 battles and 50 spreadsheets each rated by all five experts: 134 versus 250 evaluations. v2 also adds a circulation question and a blinded pairwise follow-up in which five experts each assess 25 battles. Generation temperatures and token limits remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds correlations between failure-tag rates and model win rates to examine arena blind spots (Table 4), a direct pairwise expert follow-up testing preference alignment, sensitivity to alternative multiple-testing corrections, and token/cost analyses (Appendix M). These substantially extend the retained diagnostic analyses.

E5.justification: v2 adds leaderboard error bars and 95% bootstrap Elo and analytic Bradley-Terry intervals (Figure 1, Table 9), Benjamini-Hochberg and Benjamini-Yekutieli corrections, a pooled-versus-domain likelihood-ratio test, and correlation significance tests. Expert reliability is now assessed across all 50 spreadsheets rather than only 15 multiply rated cases.

E6.justification: The main leaderboard and failure-tag rates are unchanged, but finance results are replaced under the revised design: overall mean 2.87 to 2.86 and expert-arena agreement 42.3% to 56.0%. v2 newly reports 66.4% agreement in the pairwise follow-up, 16.1% circulation acceptance, correlation results and $1,244.10 cost across 9,647 generations. These are not same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The Bradley-Terry formulation, feature-augmented Equation 1, reference anchor and rounded-mean rubric score in Equation 2 retain their mathematical substance. Section 3 replaces the explicit standard cross-entropy expression with equivalent MLE prose; no substantive theory or proof change is introduced.

C1.justification: v2 adds public dataset and code release as an explicit third contribution, replacing v1's promise of a future dataset release. The central claims about the arena, model rankings, domain-dependent preferences and inadequate professional finance quality remain.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies expert-arena agreement because independent rubric ratings and pairwise choices use different elicitation procedures. It also interprets the new correlations as arena blind spots, acknowledges that many domain effects fail multiple-testing correction, and discusses computational costs. These refine the retained overall interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 supplies concrete dataset and code access links instead of a future release promise. It adds prompt-source distributions, detailed expert-review instructions including shuffled presentation, batching and review duration, and per-model token usage, providers and API costs. Existing model configuration values are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning through a finance-task evaluation discussion covering works such as BloombergGPT, FinGPT, FinQA, TAT-QA, PIXIU and FinBen. It also expands spreadsheet-specific comparisons, explicitly distinguishing declarative workbook synthesis from manipulation tasks with predefined gold answers.

P1.justification: v2 extensively compresses and rewrites the abstract, background and analysis narrative, moves domain discussions and failure-judging details into reorganized appendices, and incorporates much of the former conclusion into an expanded Impact Statement. Conflict-of-interest and funding disclosures are also added.

P2.justification: v2 adds correlation, prompt-distribution, confidence-interval and resource-use tables, introduces error bars in Figure 1, and removes v1's expert-agreement scatterplot. It relocates the academic ranking table and substantially regroups appendix displays. The spreadsheet example images themselves are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation and reproducibility: it replaces predominantly single-rated expert cases with fully crossed ratings, adds a direct pairwise check, reports ranking uncertainty and multiple-testing corrections, and provides data/code release links. These address important weaknesses in v1's support for preference and expert-comparison findings. The reduction from 52 to 25 distinct finance battles narrows case coverage, and expert reliability remains low, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger evaluation design and transparency.
